chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Sector Rotation Into Practice

lessons.title: Business Cycle Funds in India: What They Promise and How to Judge Them

body.text: A business cycle fund offers to do everything this course has taught, on your behalf. That can be a sensible outsourcing decision, but only if you judge the fund on the same evidence you would demand of yourself.

children.text: If reading the cycle, scoring indicators, and rotating sectors sounds like a lot of work, the mutual fund industry has an answer: a fund that does it for you. India now has a whole category of them. This lesson explains what these funds are, what they can and cannot deliver, and the six checks to run before trusting one with your money.
What a Business Cycle Fund Actually Is

These are thematic equity funds whose stated theme is the business cycle itself. Instead of committing to one sector, the manager shifts allocation between sectors as the cycle turns, which is exactly the framework from Chapters 2 and 3. Under SEBI rules, a thematic fund must invest at least 80% of assets in its theme, and from the February 2026 categorisation circular, thematic funds are a category separate from single-sector funds.

body.text: Treat those category averages carefully. They are for one three-year window that happened to favour cyclical and public sector heavy portfolios, they compare two different categories with different mandates, and they hide wide dispersion between the best and worst funds. A single favourable window is not evidence that cycle-based investing reliably beats a diversified fund.

children.text: The Promise and What It Requires

The pitch is appealing: professional analysts read the macro data, a manager rotates sectors, and you hold one fund through the whole cycle without paying tax on every switch. That last point is genuinely valuable. Inside a fund, the manager can rotate between sectors without creating a taxable event for you, while your own switch between two sector funds triggers capital gains tax, as Lesson 5.1 showed.

But the fund still has to get four things right in sequence, and Chapter 4 showed how hard each one is: identify the phase in real time, pick the sectors that will actually lead in that phase, time the rotation before the market prices it in, and do all that after fees. A fund that is wrong on any one of them can underperform a plain index fund for years.

body.caption: How to judge a business cycle fund

cells: Does the scheme document describe a genuine cycle process, and is the benchmark a broad index such as Nifty 500 TRI?
Compare the fund's sector weights with the benchmark's. If they barely differ, you are paying active fees for near-index exposure
How much the manager actually trades. Very low turnover suggests little rotation; very high turnover means costs and a strong bet on timing
Direct plan expense ratio, and the gap to the regular plan. Also check the exit load period
How long the current manager has run the fund, and whether the process survives a change
Performance across several periods, not one window, and how the fund behaved in market falls

children.text: Numbers help. The ICICI Prudential Business Cycle Fund reported a portfolio turnover ratio of 46% as of 29 July 2025, which implies an average holding period of a little over two years. That is consistent with cycle-based rotation rather than short-term trading: phases last quarters to years, so a cycle fund should not be churning its portfolio every few months.

body.title: Turnover to Holding Period
body.prompt: A fund reports a portfolio turnover ratio of 46% a year. As a rough approximation, what is the implied average holding period for its positions, in years? Give your answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 100 divided by 46 is about 2.2 years. The approximation is crude, because turnover is usually measured on the lower of purchases or sales and is distorted by fund inflows, but it is a useful sanity check. A cycle fund with turnover of 300% would be trading far faster than business cycle phases actually turn, which should prompt questions about the process.

children.text: Fees matter more than most investors assume. The ICICI Prudential Business Cycle Fund's direct plan carried an expense ratio of about 0.67%, against about 1.42% for the regular plan, a gap of 0.75 percentage points that buys you nothing but distribution.

body.caption: The same simplified cost model as Lesson 5.1: every year, the expense ratio comes out of the return

body.title: Direct vs Regular Over a Decade
body.prompt: You invest ₹10 lakh for 10 years in a business cycle fund. The gross return is 12% a year. The direct plan charges 0.67% and the regular plan 1.42%. How much more would the direct plan leave you with after 10 years? Give the answer in rupees, rounded to the nearest ₹10,000.
body.explanation: The direct plan grows to about ₹29,24,975 and the regular plan to about ₹27,33,794, a difference of roughly ₹1,91,180 on a ₹10 lakh investment. That is the cost of buying the same fund through a distributor rather than directly. The fund's own exit load, 1% if redeemed within one month in this case, matters far less for a long-term holding but does penalise quick exits.

body.text: Look at the tax side too. A fund manager rotating sectors inside the scheme creates no tax event for you, while your own rotation between sector funds does. For an investor who would otherwise switch sectors two or three times a year, that tax deferral can easily outweigh a higher expense ratio. For an investor who would hold one sector tilt for three years, it may not.

children.text: These are not mutually exclusive. A common structure is a diversified core, a business cycle fund as one satellite handling rotation, and perhaps one direct sector tilt where you have a strong view. What matters is that each part has a job and a size, as Lesson 5.2 set out.

body.title: Go deeper: reading a business cycle fund factsheet

content.title: Factsheet Review Checklist
steps: Compare the fund's top five sector weights with the benchmark's, and note the largest overweight and underweight
Check how those sector weights have changed over the last three or four monthly factsheets, which shows whether rotation is real
Read the fund manager commentary for an explicit view on the cycle phase, and judge whether it matches your own scorecard
Note the cash and debt allocation: a large cash position is a market timing call you may not want
Check portfolio turnover against the length of a typical cycle phase
Compare direct plan expense ratio with peers in the same category
Look at rolling returns over three and five years, not just the trailing one-year number

body.title: Name the Category
body.textWithBlank: Under SEBI's scheme categorisation, business cycle funds sit in the ___ category, which must invest at least 80% of assets in its stated theme.
body.explanation: A business cycle fund is a thematic fund: its theme is the cycle itself, and the manager may hold any sector that fits the current phase. From February 2026, SEBI treats thematic funds as a category distinct from single-sector funds.

body.title: Judge the Fund
body.question: A business cycle fund's factsheet shows sector weights almost identical to its Nifty 500 TRI benchmark for four consecutive months, with a direct plan expense ratio of 1.1%. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The fund is doing excellent risk management by matching the index
You may be paying active fees for near-index exposure, with little actual rotation happening
Sector weights do not matter for a business cycle fund
The fund must be about to rotate aggressively
body.explanation: A cycle fund earns its fee by deviating from the benchmark at the right times. Weights that match the index for months mean you are getting index-like exposure at an active fund price. That may still be acceptable if the fund deviates decisively at turning points, but it is exactly the question to ask, and a low-cost index fund is the obvious alternative.

cards.definition: An equity fund investing at least 80% of assets in a stated theme, which for a business cycle fund is the cycle itself.
How much of the portfolio is traded in a year. Roughly, 100 divided by turnover gives the average holding period in years.
The gap between a fund's sector weights and its benchmark's. The source of both outperformance and underperformance.
The version of a scheme bought without a distributor, at a lower expense ratio. The same portfolio, cheaper.
Returns measured over many overlapping periods, which reveal consistency better than a single trailing number.
A manager can rotate sectors within a scheme without creating a taxable event for investors, unlike your own switching.

body.title: Outsource or Do It Yourself?
body.scenario: Meera, 41, has a core of two diversified index funds and wants sector rotation exposure worth 15% of her portfolio. She has followed this course, keeps a monthly scorecard, but travels heavily for work and often misses her quarterly reviews. She is comparing a business cycle fund with a direct plan expense ratio near 0.7% against running two sector index fund tilts herself, which she would expect to switch about twice a year.
body.prompt: Which route fits her better, and what would you check before she commits?
body.modelAnswer: The business cycle fund probably fits her better, for two practical reasons rather than any belief that fund managers are better forecasters. First, her own plan requires disciplined quarterly reviews that she frequently misses, and a half-monitored rotation strategy is worse than none. Second, switching sector funds twice a year means repeated short-term capital gains at 20%, while a manager rotating inside a fund creates no tax event for her, which can outweigh the higher expense ratio at that switching frequency. Before committing she should run the six checks: does the scheme document describe a real cycle process; do the monthly factsheets show sector weights genuinely deviating from the Nifty 500 TRI benchmark and changing over time; is portfolio turnover consistent with cycle-length holding periods; is she buying the direct plan; how long has the manager run the fund; and how did it behave in falling markets, not just in the recent favourable three-year window. She should also size it at 15% as a satellite, and decide in advance what would make her exit, so the decision is not made during a bad quarter.

body.label: Value Research: Business Cycle Fund Category
body.description: Compare every fund in the category on returns, assets, expense ratio, and portfolio, and read the underlying portfolio disclosures.

body.text: This lesson is educational. Fund names are examples used to illustrate how the category works, not recommendations. Assets, expense ratios, turnover, and returns are as reported at the time of writing and will change, and past returns do not predict future performance. Consider consulting a SEBI registered investment adviser before investing.

points: Business cycle funds are thematic funds that rotate between sectors as the cycle turns, with at least 80% of assets in the theme
India has about 19 such funds; the oldest dates to August 2014 and the largest managed ₹16,123 crore in August 2026

The largest fund reported a since-inception return of about 20.0% a year from January 2021 to January 2026, against about 15.4% for its Nifty 500 TRI benchmark, but one window is not proof of a repeatable edge
The real advantage is tax deferral: a manager can rotate inside the scheme without creating a taxable event for you
Costs still decide a lot: a 0.75 percentage point gap between direct and regular plans is worth roughly ₹1,91,180 on ₹10 lakh over 10 years at a 12% gross return

Run six checks: mandate and benchmark, actual sector deviation, portfolio turnover (about 46% implies a holding period near 2.2 years), costs, manager continuity, and rolling returns with downside behaviour
Fund, do-it-yourself, and no tilts at all are all defensible; choose based on tax, effort, and whether you will actually follow your own process
